title: Horizontal vs Vertical Scaling
description: Compare scaling up versus scaling out with real AWS cost curves, SPOF analysis, and Instagram's journey from 3 servers to 1000.

segments.text: Let's settle the oldest debate in infrastructure engineering. When your system is buckling under load, do you buy a bigger machine or buy more machines? The answer is nuanced, and I've seen teams get it catastrophically wrong.

Vertical scaling means upgrading your existing box. More CPU cores, more RAM, faster SSDs. AWS's r6g.16xlarge gives you 64 vCPUs and 512 GB RAM at roughly eight dollars per hour. It's simple. No code changes. Your monolith just gets a faster home.

But here's the brutal ceiling. The largest EC2 instance, u-24tb1.metal, costs over a hundred dollars per hour and you still hit physics limits. Shannon's law, memory bus bandwidth, thermal throttling. There's no instance size called 'infinite.'

Horizontal scaling means adding more machines. Sixteen r6g.xlarge instances give you the same total compute as one r6g.16xlarge, at the same eight dollars per hour total. But you get something priceless: no single point of failure. One box dies, fifteen remain.

The cost curve tells the real story. Vertical scaling is cheaper until roughly four to eight cores. After that, you pay a premium for bigger boxes because specialized hardware has lower supply. At scale, horizontal wins on price per compute unit every time.
segments.thought_prompt: If horizontal is cheaper at scale, why doesn't everyone start with it from day one?

segments.text: The catch is complexity. Stateless services like API servers scale horizontally trivially. Spin up more containers behind a load balancer. No shared state, no coordination. This is why every microservices guide starts by saying 'make it stateless.'

Stateful services are the nightmare. Databases, caches, queues. When you shard a database across ten machines, you now deal with distributed transactions, cross-shard joins, and rebalancing. That's months of engineering, not a config change.

Instagram's story is the perfect case study. Launch day in 2010: three servers. One Django app server, one PostgreSQL database, one for photos on S3. By acquisition in 2012, they had over a thousand servers serving forty million users, with just thirteen engineers.

Their key insight: scale vertically first for the database, horizontally for app servers. They vertically scaled PostgreSQL until they couldn't, then sharded by user ID. App servers were stateless from day one. They never prematurely distributed what didn't need distributing.

The single point of failure argument clinches it for production systems. Your vertically-scaled database is a ticking time bomb. Hardware fails. AWS instances get retired. When your one big box goes down at two AM, your entire platform is dark.
segments.thought_prompt: What's the blast radius when your single database server has a hardware failure?

segments.text: Here's the framework I use. Start vertical. It's simpler, cheaper, and faster to market. Monitor your ceiling. When you're at sixty percent capacity on your largest available instance, start planning horizontal. Design stateless from the start, even if you deploy on one box.

The real answer isn't horizontal or vertical. It's both, applied to different layers at different stages of growth. Your app tier scales out. Your database scales up until it can't, then you shard. This hybrid approach is how every successful system at scale actually works.
